--- title: "Regression and classification" description: "Quantities and categories, the marine outcomes that fit neither neatly, and what is lost when a count becomes present or absent." order: 1 categories: [supervised, regression, classification] --- ## The outcome decides the method Before choosing a model, decide what kind of thing the outcome is. That one decision settles which models can be used, how their errors are measured and what their predictions can be used for. This page sets out the two kinds, the marine outcomes that fit neither neatly, and what is lost when a count is turned into present or absent. ::: {.callout-note collapse="true"} ## About the data on this page The coastal survey used here is **simulated**, not a real survey. That is deliberate: because we wrote the generating process (`R/make-example-data.R`), we know the true relationships and can show whether a model recovers them. No real survey is being misrepresented, and the figures are not results about any real species. See `data/README.md` for what is built into it. ::: ::: {.callout-note collapse="true"} ## About the Python tabs Most code blocks on this page have an **R** and a **Python** tab, and picking one switches the whole page. Both run when the site is built, and each tab shows its own output. The Python tab is the scikit-learn equivalent of the R; the figures come from R throughout, and a few steps with no scikit-learn counterpart have no Python tab, which is itself worth noticing. Expect the **numbers to differ slightly** where randomness is involved: R and Python draw their random splits from different generators, so the split is not the same one. The conclusions are. ::: ## Quantities and categories [Types of learning](../01-introduction/types-of-learning.qmd) split supervised learning in two. **Regression** predicts a quantity, such as a temperature or a weight. A near miss is nearly right: predicting 11 when the truth is 12 is a small error, and predicting 20 a large one. **Classification** predicts a category, such as present or absent, or a seabed type. Most classification models give a probability for each category, and the answer is the most probable one. It is right or wrong, but the probability shows how sure the model was. ::: {.diagram} ![Regression predicts a quantity, and its error is a distance in the outcome's units. Classification predicts a category, with a probability for each.](img/two-kinds-of-outcome.svg){fig-alt="Two cards. Regression predicts a quantity, such as a temperature, a weight or a count. A number line marks the truth at 12, a prediction of 11 as nearly right and one of 20 as far off; the error is measured as a distance in the outcome's own units. Classification predicts a category, such as present or absent, a species or a seabed type. Bars give each category a probability: sand 0.6, mud 0.3, rock 0.1. The answer is right or wrong, and the probability shows how sure the model was. A note says many marine outcomes need more care than either box suggests: counts, percentages and ordered classes."} ::: ## Marine outcomes rarely fit one box Linear regression assumes the outcome can take any value, above or below zero, with the same spread everywhere. Few marine outcomes behave like that: | Outcome | Kind | What needs care | | --- | --- | --- | | Catch weight | Quantity | Skewed: a few very large catches; often modelled on a log scale | | Count of animals | Quantity | Whole numbers, never negative, spread grows with the average | | Count with many zeros | Quantity | A zero can mean the species is absent, or present and missed | | Percentage cover | Quantity | Cannot go below 0 or above 100 | | Present or absent | Category | One of the two is usually much rarer | | Habitat class | Category | Often ordered (poor, fair, good), and the order carries information | | Community composition | Neither | Shares of many species that add up to one | ## Worked example The survey counted the animals of one species at each station. That count can be treated as a quantity or turned into a category. ### The count is a quantity with a shape ::: {.panel-tabset group="language"} ## R ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} survey |> summarise( stations = n(), mean_count = round(mean(abundance), 1), variance = round(var(abundance), 1), zeros = sum(abundance == 0), zero_pct = round(100 * mean(abundance == 0), 1) ) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display}
| stations| mean_count| variance| zeros| zero_pct| |--------:|----------:|--------:|-----:|--------:| | 800| 3.9| 22.8| 180| 22.5|
::: ::: ## Python ::: {.cell} ```{.python .cell-code} import pandas as pd from mlbasic_data import load_coastal_survey_clean survey = load_coastal_survey_clean() pd.DataFrame({ "stations": [len(survey)], "mean_count": [round(survey["abundance"].mean(), 1)], "variance": [round(survey["abundance"].var(), 1)], "zeros": [int((survey["abundance"] == 0).sum())], "zero_pct": [round(100 * (survey["abundance"] == 0).mean(), 1)], }) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} | stations | mean_count | variance | zeros | zero_pct | |-----------:|-------------:|-----------:|--------:|-----------:| | 800 | 3.9 | 22.8 | 180 | 22.5 | ::: ::: ::: Two things in that summary shape every model of this count. **The variance is far larger than the mean**, 22.8 against 3.9: about 6 times. The variance measures how widely the counts spread. If animals were scattered independently of one another, the two would be about equal. They are not, because animals gather in groups, so some stations catch many and most catch few. This is called **overdispersion**, and it is normal in ecological counts. **22.5% of stations caught nothing.** A straight line predicts smooth numbers and cannot reproduce a spike at zero; it will even predict negative counts. The [next page](linear-and-polynomial-regression.qmd) shows this, and [Regression for counts](count-regression.qmd) introduces a model built for them. ### The same count as present or absent Recording only whether any animal was caught turns the count into a category. ::: {.panel-tabset group="language"} ## R ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} p_count <- ggplot(survey, aes(abundance)) + geom_histogram(binwidth = 1, fill = ml_palette[["blue"]]) + labs(x = "Animals caught", y = "Stations", title = "As a quantity: regression") p_binary <- survey |> mutate(status = if_else(abundance > 0, "present", "absent")) |> count(status) |> ggplot(aes(status, n)) + geom_col(fill = ml_palette[["orange"]], width = 0.6) + geom_text(aes(label = n), vjust = -0.4, size = 4) + scale_y_continuous(expand = expansion(mult = c(0, 0.12))) + labs(x = NULL, y = "Stations", title = "As a category: classification") p_count + p_binary ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![One measurement, two outcomes. Left: the count, with a spike at zero and a long right tail. Right: the same stations as present or absent.](regression-and-classification_files/figure-html/fig-two-framings-1.png){#fig-two-framings fig-alt='Two panels. The left panel is a histogram of the number of animals caught per station, with a tall bar at zero, a peak at one to three animals and a long tail past thirty. The right panel is a two-bar chart: absent, and present, which is over three times taller.' width=1700} ::: ::: ::: The category is simpler, but it hides how many animals each present station caught: ::: {.panel-tabset group="language"} ## R ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} survey |> filter(abundance > 0) |> summarise( `stations present` = n(), `smallest catch` = min(abundance), `median catch` = median(abundance), `largest catch` = max(abundance) ) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display}
| stations present| smallest catch| median catch| largest catch| |----------------:|--------------:|------------:|-------------:| | 620| 1| 3| 40|
::: ::: ## Python ::: {.cell} ```{.python .cell-code} caught = survey.loc[survey["abundance"] > 0, "abundance"] pd.DataFrame({ "stations present": [len(caught)], "smallest catch": [caught.min()], "median catch": [caught.median()], "largest catch": [caught.max()], }) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} | stations present | smallest catch | median catch | largest catch | |-------------------:|-----------------:|---------------:|----------------:| | 620 | 1 | 3 | 40 | ::: ::: ::: A station with one animal and a station with 40 are both simply "present". If the question is where the species occurs, that is a fair simplification. If it is where the species is abundant, the answer has been thrown away. ### Cutting a quantity loses information The opposite move is more common and does more harm: taking a quantity, choosing a cut-off and modelling the category. Split chlorophyll at 1 mg m⁻³ into "high" and "low", and a station at 0.99 lands in the same box as the lowest in the survey, 0.07, but in a different box from one at 1.01. All the variation on each side of the line is lost, and no model can get it back. Turn a quantity into a category only when the decision itself is yes or no, such as a legal limit or a protocol that records only whether a species was seen. ## The outcome sets the model and the score Once the kind of outcome is known, the rest follows: | | Regression | Classification | | --- | --- | --- | | **A first model** | Linear regression | Logistic regression | | **Output** | A number | A probability for each category | | **Error measured by** | How far off, on average (RMSE) | How often it is wrong | Some methods, such as the decision trees later in this section, do both. In tidymodels the choice is then one argument, `set_mode("regression")` or `set_mode("classification")`, which makes it easy to change the scientific question without noticing. ## Key points ::: {.key-points} - Decide what kind of outcome you have before choosing a model: a quantity means regression, a category means classification. - Many marine outcomes need more care than either box suggests: counts, percentages, ordered classes and shares. - The survey's count is overdispersed, its variance about 6 times its mean, and 22.5% of stations caught nothing. - Turning a count into present or absent keeps where a species occurs and loses how abundant it is. - Cut a quantity into categories only when the decision itself is yes or no. ::: ## Try it yourself 1. Compute the mean and variance of `abundance` for each `substrate`. Is the count overdispersed on every seabed type, or on some more than others? 2. Split `chlorophyll_mg_m3` at 1 mg m⁻³ and find the two stations closest to the line on either side. How different are they, and how different are the lowest and highest stations in the same box?
